input.summary: Jason Ku opens an introduction to algorithms course, taught with two other faculty instructors. He says the course is about solving computational problems, proving correctness, arguing efficiency, and communicating these ideas clearly, so students will write more than they code. He then defines a computational problem formally as a binary relation between a set of inputs and a set of outputs, usually specified by a checkable predicate. He stresses that the course targets general problems with arbitrarily sized inputs, using a birthday-matching example. He begins to contrast an algorithm, a fixed-size procedure that maps any input to a correct output, with a problem specification.

chapters.title: Arbitrary input sizes and what an algorithm is

keyPoints: The course is about solving computational problems, proving correctness, arguing efficiency, and communicating solutions.
Expect more writing than coding; the course is compared to a communication-intensive class.
A computational problem is a binary relation (a bipartite graph) between possible inputs and possible outputs.
An input may have several correct outputs, for example any index holding the value five.
Problems are usually defined by a predicate that checks whether an output is correct for a given input.
The course wants deterministic algorithms, not probabilistic ones.
Algorithms should be general and handle arbitrarily large inputs, not one fixed instance like a single classroom.
An algorithm is a fixed-size procedure that, given any input, produces one of the correct outputs.
